newsitem.title: FRANCE: Club Med rallies, analysts raise ratings.
newsitem.headline: Club Med rallies, analysts raise ratings.

text.p: Shares in Club Mediterranee rose on Friday after the founding Trigano family quit the company which pioneered all-inclusive, fun-in-the-sun vacations, leaving a more profit-oriented management at the helm, analysts said.

"The Triganos focused on the product. Chairman Philippe Bourguignon sees that it's a good product, but poorly sold," said analyst Antoine Nodet at French brokerage Natexis. He raised his rating on the stock to B2, or outperform, from B1.
"The Triganos are gone and we're set for a new era," said Paribas analyst Nigel Reed, who put a buy rating on the share and expects it to outperform the bourse by up to 25 percent.
"There's a huge upside potential in terms of profit if the new management can sell and market the product and increase occupancy levels," Reed said.
The stock was up 5.93 percent at 445 francs at 1335 GMT, while the bourse's CAC-40 index was down more than two percent.

Club Med, which announced restructuring plans last February at the behest of the biggest shareholder, the Agnelli family's Exor holding company, took an additional 630 million francs ($104 million) of restructuring charges in the 1996/97 first half and reported a 413 million franc loss.
It said it may have to take more provisions in the second half but not as much as the 630 million taken in the first half.
"Bourguignon is trying to sweep out all the rubbish," Reed said. "He wants the 1998 numbers to look good -- that's the first year for which he will be responsible."
Serge Trigano, who had been kicked upstairs in February to an honorary post on the supervisory board, quit on Friday along with his father Gilbert, who co-founded the firm in 1950.

"The new team has its own methods which are not mine," Serge Trigano told Europe 1 radio. "I don't know if it will be a Mickey Club or something else but it will certainly be a different club from the past and it's not my club."
His remarks alluded to Bourguignon's previous job heading Euro Disney, which he turned into Europe's top tourist attraction.
Bourguignon said on Friday that he wanted to revitalise Club Med and spruce up the resorts while preserving the powerful brand identity and culture.

"The Club has fantastic potential which is largely under-exploited today due to multiple weaknesses," he said in a letter to shareholders. "Club Med is a great brand ... It needs to preserve its culture but change its operating methods."

He outlined a two-phase plan for the company after cleaning up the balance sheet this year. The company will strive in the first phase, between now and 1999, to lure back customers with attractive prices made possible by strict cost controls.
From 2000 to 2002, it plans to step up the pace of new resort openings and new product offerings.
"This is a company that is growing, not one that's selling cruise ships, closing vacation villages," Bourguignon said, chiding the previous management's retrenchment moves.
Brokerage Meeschaert-Rousselle reaffirmed a buy rating on Club Med's stock. "When Bourguignon puts his mind to something, he follows through," said an analyst at the firm.
Analysts broadly agreed that the Club Med concept was valid.
"What could be nicer than going to an exotic spot by the sea, with fabulous food and a convivial atmosphere, with young people and all the sports facilities?" Reed said.
"They have a fabulous array of villages in wonderful locations. What they've got to do is go out and sell these holidays," he said.
-- Christine Tierney, Paris Newsroom, +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 6.056 French Francs)
